chunks: "The honest answer is that it's a trade-off between isolating noise and keeping return paths short.
If you split analog, digital and power grounds, you stop noisy digital or motor return currents from flowing through the quiet analog copper, which can help in low-frequency, high-resolution systems.

But every signal that crosses between the sections needs a return path, and across a split that path has to go around to the bridge, which makes a big loop, adds inductance and crosstalk, and radiates.

A single solid plane gives every signal its own low-inductance return right underneath it, and is simpler and more robust, but if you place things carelessly the noisy return currents can mix with the quiet ones.

So my default is one solid ground plane, with the board partitioned by placement: power stage and digital in one area, the analog front end in another, and the ADC at the boundary so digital signals don't have to travel through the analog area.
I'd only separate grounds physically when there's a real reason, like very high power currents, a precision low-frequency sensor, or galvanic isolation.
Then I'd join them at one deliberate point, under the converter or at the power entry, and route no signals across the gap except over that bridge."
